hints.junior: No autocomplete attribute meant the password manager never offered to generate or save a password — the user typed it by hand and had nothing saved to log back in with.
hints.mid: Browsers don't read label text to guess a field's purpose — that's for humans, not autofill.
hints.staff: Unreliable password autofill pushes people toward typing or copy-pasting passwords by hand, which is worse for security, not neutral.

hints.junior: Same-looking form, same labels — only the autocomplete attribute differs between the two modes.
hints.mid: Broken mode's fields have nothing for autofill to key off; fixed mode's tokens tell it exactly what each field is.
hints.staff: No real password-manager API can be scripted from a public page, so this simulates the same present/correct-token → fill, absent/generic → skip decision the real thing makes.

hints.junior: current-password for login forms, new-password for signup/change-password forms — that's the pair that matters most.
hints.mid: new-password on both the password and confirm fields signals 'this is where a new one gets created,' which is also the cue managers use to offer generating a strong one.
hints.staff: autocomplete='on' or a missing value isn't 'figure it out' — most browsers just decline to fill sensitive fields rather than guess wrong.

hints.junior: Email, phone, name, address, and payment fields all have their own specific autocomplete tokens, not just passwords.
hints.mid: A confirm-password field left without new-password (or copy-pasted as current-password) can get autofilled with an old saved password by mistake.
hints.staff: autocomplete='off' doesn't reliably block saving on password fields in modern browsers — a fresh, unseen name attribute is the mechanism that actually works for that.

sections.junior: A signup form had password fields with no autocomplete attribute at all, so a password manager never offered to generate a strong password for it. The user typed one by hand, and when they came back later to log in, there was nothing saved to autofill.
sections.mid: Browsers don't read a field's label or placeholder to figure out what it's for, that's meant for humans, not for autofill. Without the right attribute, the field's purpose is just ambiguous.
sections.staff: This really matters for security, because unreliable autofill pushes people who rely on a password manager toward typing or copy pasting passwords by hand instead, which is a worse habit, not a neutral one.

sections.junior: The autocomplete attribute takes specific values that describe exactly what a field is for, current password for logging in, new password for signing up or changing one, one time code for a verification step.
sections.mid: Use new password on both the password and confirm fields during signup, that tells the manager not to fill an old saved value and instead offer to generate a fresh strong one.
sections.staff: Turning autocomplete on or just leaving it off isn't the same as letting the browser figure it out, most browsers would rather skip filling a sensitive field than risk guessing wrong.

sections.junior: Click simulate autofill on the same looking login form in each mode and see what happens, the labels are identical, only the attribute underneath is different.
sections.mid: In broken mode there's nothing for autofill to key off of, so it can't identify the fields. In fixed mode the real tokens are there and it fills correctly.
sections.staff: There's no real password manager API you can script from a public demo page, so this mirrors the actual decision, a correct token gets filled, a missing or generic one gets skipped.

sections.junior: A password field with no autocomplete value, or the wrong one, just doesn't get autofilled or offered a generated password.
sections.mid: Give every autofill relevant field its specific token, labels and placeholders are for people, autocomplete is what autofill actually reads.
sections.staff: Don't rely on turning autocomplete off to block saving on password fields, modern browsers mostly ignore that, and a fresh unseen field name is the mechanism that actually works instead.
